claim: Cabo Verde was uninhabited before settlement in ~1460 by Portuguese colonizers and enslaved peoples from the Senegambian region of West Africa.
source: The Republic of Cabo Verde is an archipelago off the coast of Senegal and was uninhabited before settlement in ~1460 by Portuguese colonizers and enslaved peoples from the Senegambian region of West Africa (Fernandes et al., 2003; Beleza et al., 2012; Verdu et al., 2017; Korunes et al., 2020), henceforth referred to as 'European' and 'West African' source populations, respectively.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to historical and genetic studies

claim: Settlement of Cabo Verde occurred approximately 19-22 generations ago assuming a 25- to 28-year human generation time.
source: This is approximately 19–22 generations ago assuming a 25- to 28-year human generation time (Fenner, 2005).
evidence: Calculation based on cited generation time estimate

claim: Admixture in Cabo Verde likely began within the last ~20 generations.
source: Recent analyses using genetic ancestry information alongside historical data confirmed that admixture in Cabo Verde likely began within the last ~20 generations (Korunes et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent genetic and historical analysis

claim: The malaria parasites Plasmodium vivax, P. falciparum, and P. malariae have been reported across the islands of Cabo Verde since settlement.
source: The malaria parasites Plasmodium vivax, P. falciparum, and P. malariae have been reported across the islands of Cabo Verde since settlement; recurrent malaria epidemics have primarily occurred in highly populated regions (World Health Organization et al., 2012; DePina et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to WHO and epidemiological reports

claim: Santiago has experienced the most substantial burden of malaria transmission since settlement ~20 generations ago.
source: Santiago, which has consistently been the most densely populated of the Cabo Verde islands, has experienced the most substantial burden of malaria transmission since settlement ~20 generations ago.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: Personal and historical accounts described Santiago as the most 'sickly' and 'malarious' island.
source: Personal and historical accounts of malaria incidence within Cabo Verde described the largest and most populous island, Santiago, as the most 'sickly' and 'malarious' (Patterson, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to historical account

claim: In the last century, malaria epidemics of both P. vivax and P. falciparum have occurred primarily in Santiago.
source: In the last century, malaria epidemics of both P. vivax and P. falciparum have occurred primarily in Santiago (Snow et al., 2012; World Health Organization et al., 2012; Ferreira, 2017; DePina et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies

claim: The protective Duffy-null allele is almost fixed in West African populations and rare elsewhere.
source: The protective allele is almost fixed in West African populations and rare elsewhere (Howes et al., 2011; Gething et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to population genetic studies

claim: The malaria parasite P. vivax uses the chemokine receptor encoded by the DARC gene to enter and infect red blood cells.
source: The malaria parasite P. vivax uses the chemokine receptor encoded by the DARC gene to enter and infect red blood cells.
evidence: Established biological mechanism

claim: The Duffy-null allele is protective against P. vivax infection via a single nucleotide polymorphism that disrupts binding of an erythroid-specific transcription factor in the promoter region.
source: The Duffy-null allele (also known as FY*O, rs2814778) is protective against P. vivax infection via a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) that disrupts binding of an erythroid-specific transcription factor in the promoter region (Mercereau-Puijalon and Ménard, 2010; Gething et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to molecular studies

claim: Individuals carrying the Duffy-null allele have reduced expression of Duffy antigens on the surface of the blood cell, protecting against P. vivax infection.
source: Thus, individuals carrying the null allele have reduced expression of Duffy antigens on the surface of the blood cell, protecting against P. vivax infection.
evidence: Logical inference from the mechanism described and established knowledge

claim: Duffy-null has been estimated to be under one of the strongest selective pressures in human history.
source: Duffy-null is a classic example of strong selection in the human lineage, and it has been estimated to be under one of the strongest selective pressures in human history (Hamblin and Di Rienzo, 2000; Hamblin et al., 2002; Kwiatkowski, 2005; McManus et al., 2017), suggesting it is a plausible selective pressure in Cabo Verde.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to selection studies

claim: A 1721 voyage record reported that a disease in Santiago is 'dangerous to strangers' during the rainy season.
source: Interestingly, this hypothesis goes back to a voyage in 1721 in which Captain Roberts, 1745 reported that a disease in Santiago is 'dangerous to strangers' during the rainy season.
evidence: Supported by citation to historical record

claim: Historical records suggest that foreign visitors and residents of European descent suffered more from malaria in Santiago than the African and Afro-Portuguese majority.
source: Consistent with ancestry-mediated protection from malaria, the record has been interpreted by medical historians to suggest that 'foreign visitors and residents of European descent seem to have suffered more than the African and Afro-Portuguese majority' from malaria in Santiago (Patterson, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to historical interpretation

claim: The DARC locus has the highest frequency of West African ancestry in Santiago, occurring at 0.834 frequency compared to mean West African ancestry of 0.730.
source: Within Santiago, this locus has the highest frequency of West African ancestry in the population, occurring at 0.834 frequency compared to mean West African ancestry across SNPs for individuals from Santiago of 0.730.
evidence: Calculated from genetic data analyzed in the study

claim: The DARC locus is not an outlier in its frequency of West African ancestry on Fogo or the NW Cluster, occurring at the 75th and 65th percentiles respectively.
source: In contrast, the DARC locus is not an outlier in its frequency of West African ancestry on the other island regions, occurring at the 75th and 65th percentiles for Fogo and the NW Cluster, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from genetic data analyzed in the study

claim: The DARC locus is an outlier for high West African-related ancestry in Santiago, but not Fogo or the Northwest Cluster.
source: The DARC locus is an outlier for high West African-related ancestry in Santiago, but not Fogo or the Northwest Cluster.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and stated in figure caption

claim: Under neutrality, the expected frequency of the Duffy-null allele in each Cabo Verdean population is approximately equal to the West African ancestry contribution.
source: The Duffy-null allele is nearly fixed in the West African source population and largely absent in the European source population; therefore, under neutrality, the expected frequency of the allele in each Cabo Verdean population is approximately equal to the West African ancestry contribution.
evidence: Based on population genetic theory and observed source population frequencies

claim: The Duffy-null allele is contained on all West African ancestry tracts spanning the DARC locus and not found on any European ancestry tracts.
source: As expected from source population allele frequencies, the Duffy-null allele is contained on all West African ancestry tracts spanning the locus and not found on any European ancestry tracts.
evidence: Observed in genetic data analysis

claim: West African ancestry tracts spanning the DARC locus are longer and in higher frequency than European ancestry tracts covering the region.
source: Consistent with recent selection, West African ancestry tracts are longer and in higher frequency than European ancestry tracts covering the region.
evidence: Observed in genetic data analysis

claim: The median West African ancestry tract length spanning the DARC locus is ~85 Mb, while the median European tract length is ~39 Mb.
source: The median West African ancestry tract length spanning the locus is ~85 Mb, while the median European tract length is ~39 Mb.
evidence: Calculated from genetic data

claim: The DARC gene is contained in the window with the lowest iDAT score in the genome in Santiago (window iDAT score = −2.602).
source: Notably, in Santiago, the DARC gene is contained in the window with the lowest iDAT score in the genome (Figure 2C; window iDAT score = −2.602).
evidence: Calculated from genetic data and shown in Figure 2C

claim: iDAT scores near the DARC locus are not outliers in other island regions.
source: iDAT scores near the DARC locus are not outliers in other island regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in supplementary figure

claim: The values for ancestry-based summary statistics for Santiago lie outside expectations from neutral simulations for all demographic models considered.
source: The values for the summary statistics for Santiago generally lie outside our expectations for all models, especially considered jointly (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparison of observed data to simulation results

claim: The commonly used statistic iHS does not detect significant signatures of selection at the Duffy-null SNP position.
source: That is, the commonly used statistic iHS does not detect significant signatures of selection at the Duffy-null SNP position.
evidence: Result from iHS analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: The absolute iHS values for all islands at the Duffy-null SNP are low.
source: The absolute iHS values for all islands at the Duffy-null SNP are low.
evidence: Observed in Figure 3

claim: The estimate of selection coefficient from ABC is consistent with those estimated under the deterministic population-genetic model.
source: This estimate of selection coefficient is consistent with those estimated under the deterministic population-genetic model.
evidence: Comparison of results from two different methods

claim: The ABC median estimate of initial West African ancestry contribution is 0.690, with the middle 50 percentile in [0.682,0.697].
source: The median of the posterior of initial contributions from West Africa is 0.690, with the middle 50 percentile of observed values in [0.682,0.697] (Figure 5A).
evidence: Result from ABC inference shown in Figure 5A

claim: The observed mean ancestry in Santiago is 0.737.
source: In contrast, the observed mean ancestry in Santiago (Figure 1B) is 0.737.
evidence: Calculated from genetic data

claim: The ABC estimates of initial contributions from West Africa are lower than the mean ancestry currently observed in Santiago.
source: However, our ABC estimates of the initial contributions from West Africa are lower than the mean ancestry currently observed in Santiago.
evidence: Comparison of ABC results to observed data

claim: Selection at a single locus on chromosome 1 increases ancestry proportion on chromosomes 2-22.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, mean ancestry on chromosomes 2–22 also increases with selection strength (gray), indicating that global ancestry increases beyond the contribution of higher ancestry on the selected chromosome alone (black).
evidence: Result from whole-genome simulations shown in Figure 5B

claim: Strong selection at the DARC locus over 20 generations may have skewed global ancestry in Santiago.
source: Together, this evidence suggests that strong selection at the DARC locus over 20 generations may have skewed global ancestry in Santiago and raises potential biases with a statistic that is often used to infer neutral demographic histories.
evidence: Inference from simulation results and observed data

claim: Admixture can facilitate adaptation in merely tens of generations in humans.
source: Using adaptation to malaria in the admixed population of Cabo Verde as a case study, we have demonstrated that admixture can facilitate adaptation in merely tens of generations in humans.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings

claim: The estimated selection strength is consistent with other studies that inferred selection for Duffy-null ranging from ~0.04 in sub-Saharan African populations to ~0.07-0.2 in a Malagasy population.
source: Our estimate is consistent with other studies that have inferred the strength of selection for Duffy-null ranging from ~0.04 (modeled under additive selection) in sub-Saharan African populations (McManus et al., 2017) and ~0.07 (modeled as recessive) to ~0.2 (modeled as dominant) in a Malagasy population with admixed African ancestry (Hodgson et al., 2014; Pierron et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison to cited studies

claim: The estimated strength of selection for Duffy-null is among the highest inferred for a locus in any human population.
source: Our estimated strength of selection for Duffy-null is among the highest inferred for a locus in any human population.
evidence: Comparison to broader literature on selection in humans

claim: Introgression of an adaptive allele can facilitate adaptation on short timescales, particularly for traits with large effects from single loci.
source: Introgression of an adaptive allele can facilitate adaptation on short timescales, particularly for traits with large effects from single loci.
evidence: General principle from population genetics

claim: When ancestry contributions from multiple sources are high, selection post-admixture can be a faster mode of adaptation, similar to selection on standing variation.
source: When ancestry contributions from multiple sources are high, such as is common in recent human admixture, selection post-admixture can be a faster mode of adaptation, similar to selection on standing variation (Hermisson and Pennings, 2005; Hedrick, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work

claim: Commonly used ancestry outlier approaches have identified candidate regions for admixture-enabled adaptation in many populations.
source: Commonly used ancestry outlier approaches have identified candidate regions for admixture-enabled adaptation in many populations; for example, at the HLA and LCT regions in Bantu speaking populations (Patin et al., 2017), the MHC locus in Mexicans (Zhou et al., 2016), and adaptation to high-altitude at EGLN1 and EPAS1 in Tibetans (Jeong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Drift post-admixture may substantially change allele frequencies and the distribution of local ancestry within and between individuals.
source: However, results from this framework alone can be difficult to interpret because drift post-admixture may substantially change allele frequencies and the distribution of local ancestry within and between individuals (Bhatia et al., 2014; Belbin et al., 2018; Calfee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and empirical studies

claim: Recessive deleterious variation masked by heterosis can cause a signal of increased introgressed ancestry, especially in regions of low recombination.
source: Further, recessive deleterious variation masked by heterosis can similarly cause a signal of increased introgressed ancestry, especially in regions of low recombination (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical study

claim: Outlier approaches may have increased rates of false-positive detection of regions under selection.
source: As a result, outlier approaches may have increased rates of false-positive detection of regions under selection.
evidence: Inference from the limitations described

claim: The Cabo Verdean populations have high levels of genetic divergence between European and West African source populations, improving local ancestry assignment accuracy.
source: Further, the European and West African source populations have high levels of genetic divergence for human populations, improving local ancestry assignment accuracy.
evidence: General knowledge about population divergence and its effect on ancestry inference

claim: The Duffy-null allele shows extreme geographic differentiation, being nearly fixed in sub-Saharan African populations and mostly absent in non-African populations.
source: The Duffy-null allele shows extreme geographic differentiation, being nearly fixed in sub-Saharan African populations and mostly absent in non-African populations (Mercereau-Puijalon and Ménard, 2010; Howes et al., 2011; Gething et al., 2012 ), and multiple populations with ancestry from sub-Saharan Africa show evidence for admixture-enabled adaptation throughout human history at the DARC locus (Hodgson et al., 2014; Triska et al., 2015; Busby et al., 2017; Laso-Jadart et al., 2017; Pierron et al., 2018; Fernandes et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to population genetic studies

claim: The Duffy-null allele has well-characterized functional protection against P. vivax.
source: Further, the Duffy-null allele has well-characterized functional protection against P. vivax, a malaria parasite with a documented record of recurrent transmission in Santiago since settlement.
evidence: Established from functional studies and epidemiological records

claim: Selection at the DARC locus may have affected patterns of ancestry genome-wide.
source: We demonstrated how selection at the DARC locus may have affected patterns of ancestry genome-wide (Figure 5).
evidence: Demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 5

claim: Individuals with higher genome-wide proportions of ancestry from the source population carrying the beneficial allele are more likely to have a selective advantage in early generations post-admixture.
source: Individuals with higher genome-wide proportions of ancestry from the source population carrying the beneficial allele are more likely to have a selective advantage in early generations post-admixture as recombination has yet to uncouple global ancestry proportion and the local ancestry of the selected allele (Pierron et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation and logical inference

claim: The genome-wide consequences of adaptation at a single-locus were previously proposed by Pierron et al., 2018.
source: The genome-wide consequences of adaptation at a single-locus were previously proposed by Pierron et al., 2018.
evidence: Citation to prior work

claim: The scale of simulations in Pierron et al., 2018 was limited, and the extent of the effect on the selected chromosome versus the rest of the genome was not explored.
source: However, the scale of simulations was limited, and the extent of this effect on the selected chromosome versus the rest of the genome was not explored.
evidence: Critique of prior work

claim: Selection on an allele on chromosome 1 increases ancestry proportion on chromosomes 2-22.
source: Using whole-genome simulations, we demonstrated that selection on an allele on chromosome 1 increases ancestry proportion on chromosomes 2–22; that is, the increase in global ancestry is not exclusively owing to an increase in ancestry on the selected chromosome (Figure 5B).
evidence: Result from whole-genome simulations

claim: The effect of selection on global ancestry can be detected over a range of moderate to strong selection coefficients.
source: We also showed that this effect can be detected over a range of moderate to strong selection coefficients.
evidence: Result from simulations across parameter ranges

claim: Global ancestry is often used to infer initial admixture contributions.
source: Therefore, since global ancestry is often used to infer initial admixture contributions, these and related demographic inferences may be biased under the common assumption that genome-wide patterns of ancestry reflect demography alone.
evidence: Common practice in population genetics

claim: Demographic inferences may be biased under the assumption that genome-wide patterns of ancestry reflect demography alone.
source: Therefore, since global ancestry is often used to infer initial admixture contributions, these and related demographic inferences may be biased under the common assumption that genome-wide patterns of ancestry reflect demography alone.
evidence: Inference from the study's findings about selection affecting global ancestry

claim: In the absence of negative selection, ancestry is not expected to revert to initial admixture proportions after selection is relaxed.
source: In the absence of negative selection, ancestry is not expected to revert to initial admixture proportions.
evidence: Based on population genetic theory

claim: After selection is relaxed, the population will evolve neutrally with the new ancestry proportion.
source: Instead, drift will not change global ancestry in a specific direction, and the population will evolve neutrally with this new ancestry proportion (Pierron et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on population genetic theory and cited work

claim: Difference in observed and simulated global ancestry may be caused by sampling, estimation method, demographic model misspecification, different rates of migration over time, or drift.
source: Difference in observed and simulated global ancestry may be caused by a variety of statistical and evolutionary processes beyond selection, including sampling, estimation method, demographic model misspecification, different rates of migration over time, or drift.
evidence: Discussion of alternative explanations

claim: Only mutations with large effects, such as the Duffy-null allele, are likely to show significant allele frequency deviations or ancestry-based signatures of selection in just 20 generations.
source: Further, only mutations with large effects, such as the Duffy-null allele, are likely to show significant allele frequency deviations or ancestry-based signatures of selection in just 20 generations.
evidence: Based on population genetic theory about detection power

claim: A cluster of extreme negative iDAT values was observed on chromosome 16 [~chr16: 48,000,000–60,000,000].
source: We also observed a cluster of extreme negative iDAT values on chromosome 16 [~chr16: 48,000,000–60,000,000] that may be of interest for future study.
evidence: Observed in the data analysis

claim: The chromosome 16 region with extreme iDAT values does not show high proportions of West African ancestry compared to the genome-wide distribution.
source: That said, we note that this region does not show high proportions of West African ancestry compared to the genome-wide distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed in supplementary figure

claim: The extreme iDAT values in the chromosome 16 region may be influenced by its adjacence to the centromere.
source: The extreme iDAT values in this region may be influenced by its adjacence to the centromere, which may affect the length of ancestry tracts.
evidence: Speculation based on genomic features

claim: iDAT should be used as one line of evidence alongside other summaries of variation.
source: Generally, we suggest that iDAT should be used as one line of evidence alongside other summaries of variation, such as those used in our ABC estimation and expected allele frequency calculations.
evidence: Recommendation based on methodological considerations

claim: With admixture between two source populations, it is difficult to distinguish between positive selection for one ancestry and negative selection for the other ancestry.
source: Analogous to biallelic selection scenarios, with admixture between two source populations, it is difficult to distinguish between positive selection for one ancestry and negative selection for the other ancestry.
evidence: Methodological limitation based on population genetic principles

claim: Ancestry-based methods are best suited for scenarios wherein frequencies of a selected allele differ greatly between source populations.
source: Another important limitation for ancestry-based methods of detecting selection in admixed populations is that they are best suited for scenarios wherein frequencies of a selected allele differ greatly between source populations, as is the case with Duffy-null.
evidence: Methodological limitation discussed

claim: The framework developed is broadly applicable to detect and characterize selection in other recently admixed human and non-human populations.
source: The framework developed here is broadly applicable to detect and characterize selection in other recently admixed human and non-human populations.
evidence: Claim about the generalizability of the methods

claim: The ABC approach may be extended to infer the timing of selection and admixture as well, as the tract length distribution is informative about these parameters.
source: Additionally, while the timing of admixture in Cabo Verde is well documented, our ABC approach may be extended to infer the timing of selection and admixture as well, as the tract length distribution is informative about these parameters (Gravel, 2012; Liang and Nielsen, 2014; Korunes et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to methodological papers

claim: There is a need to jointly infer selection and demographic histories.
source: Indeed, we demonstrated the need to jointly infer selection and demographic histories.
evidence: Conclusion from the study's findings

claim: The study used SNP array data from 564 admixed individuals across the island regions of Cabo Verde.
source: For this study, we used SNP array data from Beleza et al., 2013 which included 564 admixed individuals across the island regions of Cabo Verde.
evidence: Description of data used in the study

claim: One individual was removed due to high missingness on chromosome 14 (11.36%).
source: This resulted in removal of one individual with high missingness on chromosome 14 (11.36%).
evidence: Data filtering step described

claim: The final merged data set contained 884,656 autosomal SNPs.
source: The final merged data set contained 884,656 autosomal SNPs.
evidence: Description of final data set

claim: Average missingness by SNP was 0.0017.
source: Average missingness by SNP was 0.0017.
evidence: Data quality metric

claim: Phasing with SHAPEIT2 yielded phased genotypes at 881,279 SNPs.
source: Following the SHAPEIT documentation, we first ran SHAPEIT –check to exclude sites not contained within the reference map, followed by SHAPEIT phasing to yield phased genotypes at 881,279 SNPs.
evidence: Result of phasing analysis

claim: The mean and median genome-wide proportion of unknown ancestry in the data set were 0.0089 and 0.0083, respectively.
source: The mean and median genome-wide proportion of unknown ancestry in our data set were 0.0089 and 0.0083, respectively.
evidence: Result from local ancestry inference

claim: More than 99% of each individual's genome could be assigned as either West African or European ancestry.
source: Typically, more than 99% of each individual's genome could be assigned as either West African or European ancestry.
evidence: Result from local ancestry inference

claim: There is little historical or genetic evidence of migration from non-West African or non-European populations to Cabo Verde.
source: Coupled with the fact that there is little historical or genetic evidence of migration from non-West African or non-European populations to Cabo Verde (Carreira, 1983; Verdu et al., 2017; Korunes et al., 2020), we find it is unlikely that individuals in our data set have high proportions of recent ancestry from a non-European or non-African source population.
evidence: Supported by citations to historical and genetic studies

claim: The estimates of each individual's average genome-wide ancestry are highly correlated between ELAI and RFMix (Pearson's R = 0.9964; p < 1 × 10⁻⁸).
source: The estimates of each individual's average genome-wide ancestry are highly correlated between ELAI and RFMix (Pearson's R = 0.9964; p < 1 × 10−8).
evidence: Statistical comparison of two methods

claim: Estimates of global ancestry by individual from admixture are consistent with those of RFMix (Pearson's R = 0.9973; p < 1 × 10⁻⁸).
source: Our estimates of global ancestry by individual from admixture are consistent with those of RFMix (Pearson's R = 0.9973; p < 1 × 10−8).
evidence: Statistical comparison of two methods

claim: The island of Boa Vista was excluded from analyses due to small sample size (26 individuals).
source: The island of Boa Vista was excluded from analyses due to our small sample from the region (26 individuals), leaving a final set of 537 individuals across the three island regions considered in this study (Santiago: 172, Fogo: 129, NW Cluster: 236; Figure 1A).
evidence: Data filtering decision

claim: The SWIF(r) implementation achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.966.
source: With our ancestry-based measures, SWIF(r) achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.966, where an AUC of 1 represents a classifier with perfect skill.
evidence: Performance metric from validation shown in Figure 6

claim: There are no false positives in the SWIF(r) test set.
source: There are no false positives in test set and a high rate of false negatives.
evidence: Result from confusion matrix shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: The majority of false-negative classifications occurred with low starting admixture proportion or low selection strength.
source: The majority of false-negative classifications (i.e. classifying selection scenarios as neutral) occurred with low starting admixture proportion or low selection strength.
evidence: Observed in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B
